items.title: Predominant microbiology
items.contentHtml:
Escherichia coli in secondary peritonitis

Escherichia coli is the most common germ in secondary peritonitis, along with other enteric and anaerobic gram-negative bacilli such as Bacteroides fragilis. Polymicrobial contamination is the rule after hollow viscus perforation. In tertiary peritonitis (persistent postoperative), Enterococcus, Candida and resistant microorganisms predominate. The empirical antibiotic choice should cover Escherichia coli and anaerobes. In intraoperative cultures, the growth of Escherichia coli guides targeted therapy. Remember: in biliary peritonitis, Enterococcus coverage is less crucial than in that of colonic origin.

items.title: Main etiology
items.contentHtml:
Acute appendicitis as a cause

Acute appendicitis is the most common cause of secondary peritonitis. Other causes include perforated peptic ulcer, diverticulitis, cholecystitis, pancreatitis, and trauma. In post-surgical patients, anastomotic dehiscence is a key cause. Secondary peritonitis is defined by peritoneal inflammation due to contamination from the gastrointestinal or biliary tract. Clinically, the pain migrates from the periumbilical to the right iliac fossa, with signs of peritoneal irritation. Delay in diagnosis increases morbidity and mortality. Urgent appendectomy is the definitive treatment when appendicitis is the cause; associated diffuse peritonitis requires laparotomy or laparoscopy with lavage.

items.title: Murphy's sign
items.contentHtml:
Murphy's sign

Murphy's sign is the interruption of deep inspiration due to pain on palpation in the right upper quadrant, typical of acute cholecystitis. In biliary peritonitis secondary to complicated cholecystitis (perforation), the sign may be positive but with diffuse peritoneal irritation. On examination, it is palpated under the right costal margin during inspiration; Sudden pain prevents completing the movement. Its presence suggests gallbladder inflammation, but its absence does not exclude biliary disease. In established biliary peritonitis, generalized abdominal pain and rigidity dominate. The ultrasound Murphy sign (pain with the transducer) has high specificity. Not to be confused with Blumberg's sign (rebound) in appendicitis.

items.foco: Abdominal pain with rebound and stiffness
items.title: peritoneal syndrome
items.contentHtml:
Pain with rebound and stiffness

abdominal pain with rebound (Blumberg's sign) and involuntary muscle rigidity are the cardinal findings of peritoneal irritation. Rebound indicates inflammation of the parietal peritoneum; reflex rigidity reflex contracture of the abdominal wall. In diffuse peritonitis, the abdomen appears in a plank, with the absence of intestinal sounds. Percussion may reveal dullness in sloping areas due to effusion. Superficial palpation triggers intense pain. These signs are an indication for urgent surgery if there is perforation or ischemia. The differential diagnosis includes acute pancreatitis and renal colic; however, secondary peritonitis rapidly progresses to sepsis. Analgesia should not be delayed for fear of masking signs, according to current guidelines.

items.title: Pneumoperitoneum on x-ray
items.contentHtml:
Pneumoperitoneum

The radiography of the chest in standing or standing abdomen can show pneumoperitoneum, free air under the diaphragm, in perforation of the hollow viscus. It is visible in ~70% of gastroduodenal perforations, but in appendicitis or diverticulitis it may be absent. The free air is seen as a sickle-shaped radiolucent line between the liver and the diaphragm. Radiography in the left lateral decubitus position (lateral decubitus position) is alternative if the patient does not tolerate standing. The absence of pneumoperitoneum does not rule out perforation; CT scan is more sensitive. In secondary peritonitis, the finding of free air along with peritoneal effusion and thickening confirms the diagnosis. Massive pneumoperitoneum with severe distension indicates immediate surgery.

items.foco: Tomography: free fluid and peritoneal thickening
items.title: CT scan
items.contentHtml:
Tomography in peritonitis

Abdominal computed tomography (CT) with contrast is the test of choice in stable secondary peritonitis. Findings: free fluid in the peritoneal cavity, peritoneal thickening with enhancement, and septated collections. CT identifies the cause (appendicitis, diverticulitis, perforation) and complications such as abscesses. In the presence of free fluid and peritoneal thickening, the sensitivity for peritonitis is high. CT also guides percutaneous drainage of abscesses. In unstable patients, surgery should not be delayed by imaging. CT with oral contrast can help localize a leak, but intravenous contrast is essential. The finding of gas outside the intestinal lumen together with free fluid is pathognomonic of perforation.

items.title: Diagnostic peritoneal lavage
items.contentHtml:
Diagnostic peritoneal lavage (DPL)

Diagnostic peritoneal lavage (DPL) was a key procedure in blunt abdominal trauma, now obsolete due to tomography. It consists of inserting a catheter into the peritoneum, instilling serum, and aspirating to detect blood or intestinal contents. Positive criteria: aspiration of >10 mL of non-clotted blood, red blood cell count >100,000/mm³, white blood cells >500/mm³, or presence of bile, bacteria, or plant fibers. It was used to decide laparotomy in unstable patients. In secondary post-traumatic peritonitis, LPD can detect contamination, but CT is preferable. The procedure has a risk of visceral injury. Currently, FAST ultrasound has replaced LPD in the initial evaluation of trauma.

items.foco: Empirical antibiotic therapy: ceftriaxone plus metronidazole
items.title: Empirical antibiotics
items.contentHtml:
Empirical antibiotic therapy

Ceftriaxone (1-2 g intravenously every 24 hours) plus metronidazole (500 mg intravenously every 8 hours) is a standard empirical regimen for secondary community peritonitis. Covers enteric and anaerobic gram-negatives. Alternatives: piperacillin-tazobactam, or carbapenems in severe or nosocomial infection. In patients with beta-lactam allergy, use aztreonam plus vancomycin plus metronidazole. The duration of treatment is 4-7 days after control of the focus. The addition of antifungal (fluconazole) is reserved if there is a high risk of Candida (immunosuppression, recent surgery). Antibiotic therapy must be started early, but emergency surgery is the mainstay. Intraoperative culture allows adjustment to targeted therapy. Do not use antibiotics with anti-pseudomonal coverage in uncomplicated community peritonitis.

items.title: Surgical management
items.contentHtml:
Emergency surgery

Emergency surgery is the definitive treatment for diffuse peritonitis secondary to perforation or ischemia. The objective is to control the source of contamination (appendectomy, perforation suture, intestinal resection) and perform abundant peritoneal lavage. The approach can be open or laparoscopic depending on stability. Laparotomy is indicated if there is hemodynamic instability or generalized peritonitis. Surgery should be performed within the first 6-12 hours to reduce mortality. In fecal peritonitis, resection with ostomy is required. The decision to leave the abdomen open (laparostomy) is made if there is massive edema or the need for reexploration. Postoperative in intensive care unit. Resuscitation with fluids and antibiotics is not a substitute for controlling the outbreak.

items.foco: Multiple organ failure as a lethal complication
items.title: Multiple organ failure
items.contentHtml:
Multiple organ failure

Multiple organ failure (MOF) is the main cause of death in severe secondary peritonitis, secondary to sepsis and systemic inflammatory response. The release of cytokines (TNF-alpha, interleukin-1) causes endothelial damage, coagulopathy, and organ dysfunction. It manifests as acute respiratory distress syndrome, acute renal failure, liver dysfunction, and disseminated intravascular coagulation. Mortality exceeds 30% when three or more organs fail. The SOFA (Sequential Organ Failure Assessment) score assesses severity; an increase ≥2 points indicates sepsis. Treatment includes focus control, antibiotics, vasopressor support, and mechanical ventilation. Prevention of FOM relies on early surgery and goal-directed resuscitation. Multiple organ failure is the most feared lethal complication.

items.title: Hinchey classification
items.contentHtml:
Hinchey Classification

The Hinchey classification is used for complicated acute diverticulitis, based on intraoperative findings. Grade I: confined pericolic abscess. Grade II: distant pelvic or intra-abdominal abscess. Grade III: generalized purulent peritonitis. Grade IV: fecaloid peritonitis. Grades I and II can be managed with antibiotics and percutaneous drainage; grades III and IV require urgent surgery (resection with colostomy or primary anastomosis). The classification guides the prognosis: mortality increases with the grade. In peritonitis secondary to diverticulitis, preoperative tomography can predict the grade. Treatment of Hinchey III with laparoscopic lavage and drainage has shown variable results; resection remains the standard. The Hinchey classification is not prognostic in other causes of peritonitis.

items.title: Intraoperative culture
items.contentHtml:
Intraoperative culture

The intraoperative culture of peritoneal fluid or infected tissue allows the identification of the causative microorganism and its sensitivity, guiding targeted antibiotic therapy. It is recommended to take samples in all cases of secondary peritonitis, especially in severe patients or at risk of resistance. Results take 48-72 hours; meanwhile, empirical antibiotic therapy is used. If the culture grows Escherichia coli producing extended-spectrum beta-lactamases, it is suitable for carbapenem. In polymicrobial infections, all isolated pathogens should be covered. The culture also detects Candida in immunocompromised patients. Antibiotic de-escalation according to culture reduces toxicity and resistance. Do not take routine cultures in primary peritonitis (cirrhosis) without surgery. Intraoperative culture is mandatory if the peritonitis is nosocomial or postoperative.
